October killed the recovery. Here's what it means for tech hiring in the Midlands

The latest KPMG and REC Report on Jobs for the Midlands landed this week, and it's a reality check.

After three straight months of growth, permanent placements in our region fell sharply in October (index 45.0, down from 52.1 in September). That's the fastest drop since May. Temp billings fell too, at the steepest rate in 15 months.

What's behind it? Rising costs, economic uncertainty and slower decision making. Some businesses have simply pressed pause on hiring.

Here's what stood out to me:
Permanent vacancies have now been falling for nearly two and a half years.
Candidate availability rose at its fastest rate since March, driven mainly by redundancies.
Starting salaries still rose, reaching an eight month high.

And this is the bit I want hiring managers to really hear. Even with more candidates on the market, Software Developers are still listed as a skill in short supply for permanent roles, and AI/ML Developers for contract work.

More CVs doesn't mean more of the right people. I see it every week. Inboxes are fuller than ever, yet the genuinely strong developers are still being snapped up quickly, and they still expect to be paid properly for it.

My honest advice:
If you're hiring: don't let the headlines lull you into thinking you can take your time. The best people in a busy market get multiple offers. Move quickly when you find them.

If you're a tech professional: competition is tougher right now, so how you present yourself matters more than ever. If you've got in demand skills, you still hold real value.

There's positive news on the horizon too, with advanced manufacturing, aerospace and rail all flagged as big opportunities for the Midlands.

YOUR BIGGEST PROFESSIONAL RISK MAY NOT BE YOUR COMPETITION. It may be your own lack of BOUNDARIES.

The Nvidia story involving Jensen Huang has opened up a conversation that goes far beyond an alleged affair.
It brings together three subjects that businesses often discuss separately: personal relationships, corporate governance and geopolitics.

And I think there are some serious lessons here for anyone building a business, leading a team or operating in a position of influence.
Let's look at it.

1. The honey trap is not just about romance. It's about vulnerability.
In intelligence circles, a honey trap is a tactic in which someone uses romantic or emotional interest to gain access, influence or leverage over another person.
The uncomfortable question is: how well do we understand our own vulnerabilities?
A CEO has access to information that can influence markets, governments, investors, employees and even national interests.
Your personal decisions can therefore create professional consequences that you may never have anticipated.
Power doesn't make you immune to manipulation. Sometimes, it makes you a more attractive target.

2. Business and geopolitics are no longer separate conversations.
Nvidia isn't just another technology company. Its chips sit at the centre of the global AI race.
The US-China technology rivalry, semiconductor export restrictions, national security and corporate interests are all interconnected.
When you're operating at that level, even a seemingly personal association can invite questions about business relationships, access to information, influence and conflicts of interest.
This is an important lesson for founders and executives:
You may think you're managing a personal relationship. The world may see a potential corporate risk.

3. Workplace relationships need boundaries. Not every connection deserves access.
I am not suggesting that people shouldn't form friendships or relationships at work.
Some of the strongest professional partnerships begin with genuine personal connections.
But there is a difference between building relationships and becoming dependent on them.
There are certain things professionals should be careful about:
Don't mix personal intimacy with business negotiations.
Don't share confidential business information to build personal trust.
Don't create secret relationships with clients, vendors or people who have commercial influence over your organisation.
Don't allow personal equations to influence hiring, payments, promotions or business decisions.
Don't confuse someone's attention with their loyalty.
And never put yourself in a position where your personal choices can be used as professional leverage.
Not every relationship is a risk. But every relationship requires judgment.

4. Your dignity is an asset. Protect it like one.
This is perhaps the most important part of the conversation for me.
As professionals, we spend years building credibility.
We build networks, negotiate contracts, earn trust, establish reputations and work towards positions of influence.
And sometimes, in the pursuit of validation, attention, access or opportunity, we make choices that compromise the very reputation we've spent years building.
No business opportunity is worth losing your self-respect over.
No professional connection should require you to compromise your dignity.
And no position of power should make you believe that normal boundaries no longer apply to you.

5. No organisation should be bigger than its governance.
There is another business lesson here.
When a company becomes too dependent on one individual, even a personal controversy involving that individual can become an organisational crisis.
This is what business calls key-person risk.
A strong organisation needs independent oversight, transparent disclosure, succession planning and accountability.
A CEO may build the company, but the company must never become incapable of functioning without the CEO.
That's the difference between building an institution and building a personality cult.

My conclusion:
I've always believed that professional success is not just about how much you can build, how much money you can make or how many important people you know.
It's also about the decisions you make when nobody is watching.
The higher you climb, the more valuable your judgment becomes.
Your relationships can open doors, but poor boundaries can leave those same doors open to risks you never considered.
Build relationships. Build influence. Build wealth. Build powerful networks.
But don't build them at the cost of your dignity, your integrity or the organisation that trusts you.

Because your reputation takes years to build, but sometimes, one bad decision is enough to put the entire thing under scrutiny.

Your recruiters may already use an AI hiring tool. They just call it a feature.

It usually arrives quietly. The applicant tracking system ships an update with candidate match scores, auto-ranking, and a "top applicants" tab. It's included in the plan, so it never goes through procurement. Nobody files it under AI.

But a score that decides which resumes a human reads first is doing screening. Regulators have noticed.

Since 2023, New York City's Local Law 144 has required employers that use automated employment decision tools in hiring to get an independent bias audit within the prior year, publish a summary of the results, and notify candidates. The EU AI Act classifies AI used for recruitment and candidate evaluation as high-risk. Neither rule cares whether the tool was a line item or a checkbox.

Three questions for HR and legal this quarter:

1. Where does software rank, filter, or score candidates? Check the settings, not just the contracts. Defaults count.
2. Has anyone looked at outcomes? Compare selection rates across groups. Ask the vendor what bias testing they've done, and ask for the document, not the assurance.
3. Who owns the decision to keep it switched on? If nobody can answer, that's your finding.

This does not look good. It connects to another point someone in the industry made a few months ago: "Now our seniors start producing code again." His point was that GenAI allows senior software engineers, who have a deep knowledge of the codebase, to *write* the code faster (btw, the difference between programming and developing has never been so apparent), leveraging their knowledge of the codebase and *experience in software development* to write precise prompts. 
In parallel, companies reduce their hiring. Our students, who used to have a job contract signed before even finishing their master's degree, now might have to look for a job for some months before signing a first contract. I understand why companies want to have "GenAI fluent" juniors, but this is (IMHO) a bad calculation.
As many people also emphasize in the comments on the post below: GenAI is an amplifier, not a replacement for codebase knowledge and software development experience. Put in other words: we (higher education's teachers) can teach students *how* to ask, but if you do not know *what* to ask from your AI (including writing the agent SKILL.md file), there is no chance that something of high quality (and this includes long-term maintainability) will be produced. And for those who would argue that we do not need to write code, only specs and requirements, I believe this is just moving the problem to a different level where one mistake is even more damaging, as it has a higher amplitude (I remember my professors telling me that one mistake in the requirements is costlier to fix than one mistake in the code).

In summary, my fear (and I hope I am wrong) is that we will see a gap appear between senior developers with deep knowledge of a codebase and juniors who rely on Gen AI to do things without acquiring that knowledge. I fear that this gap will grow into a trench (if not a canyon) before we (and mostly companies) react. Now the big question is: how? How do we prevent our codebases (including open-source) from becoming unmanageable? How do we onboard junior developers so they can get to the speed of senior developers with Gen AI? How do we succeed in that shift from Human-centered (+ tools) development to Human + Gen AI (+ tools)? And (bonus), how do we do all that without covering our planet with power- and water-hungry data centers?

We have made a big bet in Quint's legal and compliance team. We’re hiring three graduates onto a three-year scheme, just as many employers cut graduate hiring because AI is doing the work juniors used to do. It may look like an odd moment to invest in entry-level talent, but the thinking says a lot about how AI is changing our profession.
  
Two things made this possible. First, under the SQE, qualifying work experience has replaced the training contract, and the breadth of work at Quint means we can offer it. Second, graduate jobs are harder to find, so I hoped to attract talented candidates who would not have considered an in-house role at a mid-sized company in a healthier cycle. 
  
Quint sets out to disrupt markets, and AI is changing how work gets done faster than most firms can adapt. People who have not yet learned the ‘old way’ bring the diversity of thought we need to make the most of that change.
  
Directors must have regard for the long-term consequences of their decisions, and the company’s impact on the community. In my view, that includes giving young people a ladder into work. 
  
AI complicates how we do this, given that it’s capable of doing much of the routine work that juniors have always learned from. Judgement, expertise and creativity are much harder to replace, and they are honed by doing that work, so a generation that leans on AI solely from day one risks missing out on the hard graft that develops them. 
  
The plan is simple: we train our graduates to do a job, and they then train an AI agent to handle the admin. After three years, Quint should have people expert in both our processes and the agents that support them. With agents taking on the routine work, our people get more interesting work much sooner.
  
The quality of applicants blew us away. We set a high bar on academics and on behaviour. We want people who ‘get after it’ and believe they ‘are the company’: who take ownership, see a problem through and seize an opportunity when it comes. 

Our chosen three used AI in the goldilocks zone: enough to sharpen their thinking, never so much that it replaced it. Those who missed the cut had either polished their work with AI until no trace of humanity was left, or not used it at all, believing they didn’t need to.

Since joining, Yasmin Murphy has shipped a live risk dashboard, Sana Arshad has out-researched an AI paper, and Amelie Privett has trained our due diligence agent.

Knowledge of the law can be taught. The behaviours we hired for are harder to teach: seeing a problem through to the end and knowing when to use a tool and when to trust their own thinking. Graduates who show them from day one are among the best investments a team can make, and any firm prepared to hire for behaviour first and teach the craft second should find no shortage of them right now.

AI in Market Access & HEOR: Will it replace jobs or create new opportunities?
  
I'm hearing more and more from candidates about AI and what it means for the future of the job market.
  
Will it reduce the number of roles? How will people adapt to new technology? And, perhaps most importantly, can AI ever replace the human touch when it comes to helping patients access medicines and medical devices?
  
I think the best way to look at this is through the lens of recruitment.
  
When computers first came along, people said recruiters wouldn't be needed. When LinkedIn arrived, we heard the same thing. Now AI is creating similar conversations.
  
Yet here we are, still recruiting, still hiring and seeing the industry evolve.
  
My view is that AI won't necessarily replace jobs; it will change what those jobs look like and where people add value.
  
Instead of spending hours on labour-intensive tasks, data entry and processing, professionals will increasingly be able to focus on what the data actually means, how it can influence decisions and where it can make a real difference.
  
In Market Access and HEOR, I believe this is particularly interesting.
  
AI can support evidence generation, health economic modelling and data analysis, but understanding the wider context, developing strategy, navigating healthcare systems and ultimately improving patient access still requires human judgement, experience and relationships.
  
I recently had a client ask whether they could find an HEOR Modeller with experience using AI.
  
That stood out to me because it wasn't about replacing the role. It was about adding a new skill set to an existing one. It's a clear example of how Pharma and Consultancies are beginning to think about the talent they need for the future.
   
If there's one thing I'm confident about, it's that the professionals who understand how to use AI effectively, and how to complement their existing expertise with it, will be well positioned in this evolving job market.
  
Perhaps AI won't make our roles less important. Perhaps it will give us more time to focus on the parts of our jobs that matter most.
  
I'd be interested to hear how others in Market Access and HEOR are seeing AI influence their roles and the skills clients are looking for.

First move the work overseas. Then automate more of it. Sell the journey as transformation.

Qantas says some corporate services will move to Accenture, mostly delivered by teams in India, followed by further automation and AI. Around 850 roles are expected to be affected, with the first changes expected by mid-2027.

Qantas cites ageing systems and says it will pursue redeployment and retraining. Modernisation is a legitimate objective. The decision still deserves scrutiny.

Can and should are different questions.

A business can move work offshore and automate tasks. Whether it should requires a better answer than a lower labour bill.

A proper business case tests service quality, retained expertise, transition costs, supplier dependency and the alternative of investing in existing staff.

An employee disappearing from payroll doesn’t, by itself, prove a productivity improvement. The work still has to be done properly, and someone carries the consequences when it isn’t.

How much of the gain improves employees’ prospects or customers’ service? How much simply improves margins? A workforce deserves more than a chain of progressively cheaper substitutes.

What bothers me about this consulting model is how easily a management choice becomes an apparent inevitability. Technology becomes the explanation, and responsibility gets harder to pin down.

When an adviser also stands to earn the delivery contract, its recommendation deserves independent challenge. The business case should survive scrutiny from someone who does not benefit from the sale.

The client’s executives own the decision. Hiring Accenture doesn’t transfer their responsibility for the workforce or the organisation’s long-term capability.

Grok Bot is marketed to work across applications and workflows. Routine consulting is an obvious place to test that promise.

If routine consulting work isn’t among the first cabs off the rank for tools like Grok Bot, I’ll go he.

Research summaries, first drafts, routine reporting and presentation assembly are obvious candidates. Clients with capable tools should ask how much of a consulting team they actually need.

Experienced judgement, difficult implementation and the courage to challenge a client still deserve payment. So does taking responsibility for the result. A logo and a polished slide deck need to earn their place.

There is something almost comic about paying a premium for advice that everyone else should cost less.

If automation reduces the effort, clients should expect a lower price or a better outcome. Otherwise, whose productivity dividend is it?

This is where consultancies are doing themselves no favours. Each pitch built around replacing people with cheaper delivery invites clients to examine the consulting firm through exactly the same lens.

If a consultancy’s strongest argument is that someone else can do the work more cheaply, it should expect its clients to ask the same question about the consultancy.

Three jobs in five years.

Would your AI screening tool put that CV through?

If it’s set up to flag short stints, that person might never get a conversation. But those dates don’t tell you whether a contract ended, a team was made redundant or someone moved because the progression they were promised never happened.

And they certainly don’t tell you what that person achieved while they were there.

I’m all for using AI to save time in recruitment. But if it flags a CV like this, I’d want someone to take a look before ruling the person out. A quick conversation about why they moved and what they want next can change how you read the whole CV.

That’s why I think there’ll always be a human element to recruitment.

Where would you draw the line between what AI can screen for and what a recruiter should decide?

AI was supposed to take the routine out of work. In hiring it did the opposite.

I've been looking for a Ruby on Rails role for three months, and the hiring market is a dumpster fire. Three months used to be enough to land something. Now it's mostly routine, on both sides of the table. This is how it looks from where I sit:

1. An ad goes up and nobody checks it. I recently saw one saying "B2B contract", but the client only hires employees. Then it gets copied to board after board, sometimes for months.
2. Layoffs add more people to the pile. Over 128,000 tech jobs were cut by early September 2026, mostly at big US companies (layoffs.fyi).
3. Candidates fight back. 62% of US job seekers tried tricks to get past automated screening, and 40% added skills or keywords they don't have (Greenhouse, 2026).
4. Recruiters can't read it all, so the ATS and AI do the first pass. 35% of recruiters say these tools make them miss strong candidates (CV-Library, April 2026). A viral post in October: a manager applied to his own team's opening with his CV under another name and was rejected in 6 minutes. The filter wanted "React.js". His CV said "React".
5. If the first person who reads your CV can't judge the work, they're doing the same job as the ATS. Same keyword checklist, just slower.
6. Most people get a template. 81% of US candidates were rejected in the past year without talking to a single person (Greenhouse). "Sorry, the position has been filled" is polite and tells you nothing. I've had a real reason maybe three times in my career. In October a company told me they'd "moved forward with a stronger match". In November they refreshed the same kind of job ad, and are still answering applicants.
7. With no reason, you guess. Too little experience? Wrong keywords? So the CV turns into a four-page detective novel. Then the one person who actually reads it, often the CTO, rejects it for the length.
8. Meanwhile 72% of employers say they struggle to find skilled talent (ManpowerGroup, 2026).
Job seekers automate too. Dozens of tools now pull jobs from many boards, score how well you fit, rewrite your CV for each ad, and sometimes apply for you. New ones keep launching, because every layoff brings new customers: their own CV gets rejected, so a tool tailors it. Tailoring raises the volume, so the ATS gets stricter. Tools learn to beat it, and the ATS tightens again. Machines fighting machines, and the point of it all, filling a role, gets lost.
None of these tools fixes the root cause: an ad nobody checked, and a rejection with no reason. That costs candidates months, and companies too: roles stay open, teams stay short, good people get filtered out. The only person it costs nothing is whoever wrote the ad.

AI didn't break hiring. We did it ourselves, and AI made it louder.

Oh, and by the way: if you're hiring a Rails engineer and you actually read CVs, my DMs are open.

The company expects higher material costs, particularly semiconductors, to have a gross impact of around €1 billion on its earnings in 2027. 

It plans to recover some of that through higher customer prices, product changes and cost cuts.


Reading this, I thought about the people responsible for securing those components.

When prices rise or supply becomes harder to secure, surely they face some difficult questions:


- Can we use a different component?
- How long would it take to change the product?
- Should we commit to a longer supplier contract?
- And what happens if we can’t pass the extra cost on to customers?


The people in procurement and supply leaders who understand the semiconductor industry can make a real difference here.

They can help the business understand where the risks are, what its options are and what each decision could mean for production and customers.


And as more industries compete for semiconductor supply, I think that combination of commercial, supply chain and semiconductor knowledge will become increasingly valuable.

How long since your board saw artificial intelligence (AI) listed in its risk register? If it never has, the risks AI brings into your business sit unowned at board level.

I think the reason is the way AI arrives. New systems normally come with a business case and a sponsor, and a register entry tends to follow from those. 

AI tends to turn up through subscriptions the business already holds, or through a habit someone picked up on their phone, so it rarely meets that process. In a hotel group that could be a pricing feature inside the revenue system, while in a creative agency it could be a note-taker the account team signed up for themselves.

The pace matters here. Figures from the Office for National Statistics show around 12% of UK firms with 10 or more people using AI in late 2023, climbing to around 35% by June 2026. Informal, or unapproved, usage is far higher, with 55% of UK workers in one security vendor's survey saying they used AI tools their employer hadn't approved. 

When Deloitte surveyed board members and executives in 56 countries in early 2025, 31% said AI wasn't on the board agenda.

AI saves time on drafting, summing up and routine questions, and alongside those gains come the risks I'd want a board to be weighing.
•	Client or company information landing in AI tools the business never signed off
•	AI features switched on inside existing software, able to reach data no one has checked
•	Hiring shortlists or client letters sent out on AI output that no person reviewed
•	Suppliers running AI across your data under terms you haven't read

Each of those can leave the business in breach of client contracts or data protection law.

The fix starts small, with one line per risk in the register your directors already read, each carrying a named owner and something to check every quarter.

If that would help before your next board meeting, message me. We can look across your business for AI already in use and draft those rows for you as part of an AI-readiness assessment. As a business certified to ISO 27001 and Cyber Essentials, we look after our own data to those standards.

Which of those four risks would your board struggle to put a name against today?
